title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Aviation
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Manchester Airports Group data published in full after the ransom was refused — airport operations untouched
items.content_text: Manchester Airports Group refused to pay, and the group calling itself FulcrumSec then published what it says is the full haul, roughly 550GB of uncompressed data, as SecurityWeek reported on 3 September. HaveIBeenPwned added 8.8 million accounts from it on 2 September: email addresses and phone numbers, with names, IP addresses, locations, browser details, vehicle registrations, parking history, and Fast Track and lounge bookings, relating to customers of Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports. MAG, which disclosed the breach on 27 August, says the records sat in a database hosted by a third party and that airport operations were not affected. How the attackers got in rests on FulcrumSec’s own claim, that admin keys sat in plain sight in the front-end JavaScript of the three airports’ websites; MAG has not confirmed it. Nothing new has emerged since: MAG’s incident page still shows 27 August as its latest update, and we found no regulator action. For airport operators the material question is custody: who holds passenger data, on whose infrastructure, and how far that estate sits from anything operational.

items.title: UK air traffic failure traced to a software defect in aircraft code allocation — NATS’ preliminary report describes a timing fault, not an attack
items.content_text: This is not a cyber incident. It is carried here, clearly labelled, because it is the aviation infrastructure story of the period and readers will reasonably have wondered. On 8 September a failure at NATS, the UK air navigation service provider, forced Heathrow to suspend arrivals and disrupted Gatwick and Manchester, affecting more than 2,000 flights across 8–9 September. NATS’ preliminary report, published on 18 September, places the cause in a small part of the National Airspace System: a software defect in the code that allocates aircraft identification codes. A code request was paused when a higher-priority task pre-empted it, and the update did not complete; Reuters quotes the report as saying that had the higher-priority request arrived “even one millisecond earlier or later, the update would have completed normally.” Restrictions lasted about six hours and clearing the backlog took more than two days. NATS says a mitigation is in place while a permanent fix is safety-tested and deployed. Chief executive Martin Rolfe, who had already ruled out cyber on 10 September, dismissed speculation of military interference and said the fault is unrelated to the 2023 outage; the early accounts blaming an anomalous military flight plan are not supported by the stated cause. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander called the failure “completely unacceptable” and has tasked the Civil Aviation Authority with an independent review of NATS’ findings, its resilience investment plans and regulatory accountability. A full report is to follow, and NATS proposes a further £1bn of investment by 2033. For aviation OT teams the lesson is availability engineering rather than attack defence: a defect that only surfaces when two tasks collide within a millisecond is exactly the kind of fault conventional testing can miss, so the useful questions are how your own flight-critical systems behave when an update stalls and how quickly you recover when one does.
tags: Context — ATC operational failure; preliminary report finds a software defect, and cyber was ruled out by the operator

items.title: Three airports stopped flying for drones inside ten days, and one of them for a flock of birds — the gap is detection, not defence
items.content_text: Brussels Airport halted traffic for roughly half an hour on the evening of Friday 12 September after a drone was sighted near the airfield; no injuries or damage were reported and movements resumed once the area was cleared, with the drone’s origin and intent unattributed. The following day Vilnius closed for 38 minutes on a drone alert that scrambled a NATO jet before the object was confirmed to be a flock of birds. Both follow the US Labor Day weekend incursion at San Diego that grounded around 400 flights, where the TSA reportedly could not identify the operator and coverage noted that US airports carry no mandatory drone-detection requirement at all. None of this is a cyberattack and none of it should be filed as one. It belongs on this page because the operational consequence is identical to an OT failure and lands on the same people: a ground stop cascades into stand and gate reallocation, jet-bridge and ramp re-sequencing, baggage re-flow and fuel and de-icing re-planning, and the decision to stop or resume is increasingly taken from software — counter-UAS detection feeds, ground-movement displays, airfield lighting control — that few airports treat as operational technology with an integrity requirement. Vilnius is the instructive one: the cost was not the drone, it was the ambiguity.

items.title: A China-linked crew is emptying self-hosted code repositories of SCADA and HMI source — and aerospace is on the victim list
items.content_text: Acronis threat intelligence, published on 13 September and reported on 14–15 September, describes a campaign it attributes with moderate confidence to a China-linked actor it calls Red Heron, exploiting a critical remote code execution flaw in the self-hosted Gitea code platform, CVE-2026-60004, since 29 July. The actor scanned 1,386 internet-facing Gitea instances across seven countries and compromised 11 organisations in five countries, by Acronis’s count (some secondary reports give higher figures) — the victim set spanning aerospace, telecommunications, government, elections and defence alongside industry. Two victims define the objective: a Taiwanese industrial-automation company whose stolen repositories covered SCADA and HMI tooling, IoT platform integrations and network-sniffer products, and a Canadian renewable-energy firm from which infrastructure maps, configuration secrets, SSH host keys and internal tokens were taken. The implant, a custom loader Acronis calls JITTERLY with an embedded Linux rootkit named SIXZUT, supports more than thirty post-exploitation commands. Nothing here is aviation-specific and no airport or airline has been named, but the pattern is the one that reaches this sector indirectly: MRO software houses, baggage and BMS integrators and ground-systems developers routinely keep deployment configurations, VPN profiles, device credentials and site diagrams in self-hosted repositories that sit outside anyone’s OT security programme. Stolen host keys and infrastructure maps are not the attack; they are the preparation for one that arrives later looking like legitimate maintenance access.
tags: Incident — State-linked source-code and credential theft from self-hosted developer infrastructure

items.title: Norway spent forty minutes convincing a rescue helicopter it was somewhere else — and the avionics never reported a fault
items.content_text: At Jammertest 2026, the annual open interference exercise on Andøya, researchers escalated a spoofing signal on 10 September until a rescue helicopter’s GPS display showed a false position out over the Norwegian Sea and a track of tight overlapping turns, while the aircraft in fact flew normally. The finding worth carrying is the detection asymmetry rather than the spectacle: jamming announces itself as signal loss and crews are trained for it, whereas spoofing leaves the receiver confidently reporting data that is internally consistent, plausible and wrong. This was a controlled test, not an in-the-wild incident, and no aircraft was endangered. It lands against a real backdrop the researchers cited — RAF aircraft encountering GPS jamming near the Russian border and daily GNSS interference over Sweden through 2026 — and it reinforces the updated jamming and spoofing guidance EASA issued to operators in July 2026. For airport operators the read-across runs past the flight deck. GNSS is not only a navigation input; it is a cheap and widely deployed time source, and GNSS-disciplined clocks quietly underpin surveillance feeds, surface-movement and logging across ground estates. A time source that can be walked rather than broken is a category of failure most airport OT inventories have never recorded. One defensive development came out of the same exercise: Splash247 reported on 17 September that ESA tested Galileo’s Signal Authentication Service (SAS), working alongside OSNMA, during Jammertest. Five operational Galileo satellites broadcast encrypted signals for two hours; under spoofing, conventional receivers reported false positions while SAS-equipped receivers detected the interference. Further testing and accreditation come first, and the initial service — free and worldwide — is due in 2027, so this belongs on the receiver roadmap rather than in today’s mitigation.

items.title: August set a global ransomware record at 997 attacks, with utilities among the categories driving the rise
items.content_text: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — an average of 32 a day, a 23 percent increase on July’s 809, and above the previous monthly record of 988. The reporting singles out utility, healthcare and business-services attacks as the categories behind the surge. Treat the absolute number with the usual caution — counts of this kind depend on leak-site claims and disclosure practice as much as on actual incident volume, and claimed victims are not confirmed victims. The direction of travel, however, is consistent with what operators are seeing. Airlines, airports and their service providers sit inside the business-services and transport categories driving this figure. Aviation's recent history is consistent: the encryption lands on a shared IT provider or a back-office system, and the visible failure is at check-in, baggage or turnaround rather than in a control system.

items.title: Cyber-informed engineering argues the useful question is not how to keep attackers out, but which consequences you can design away
items.content_text: An analysis published 15 September sets out the case for cyber-informed engineering in critical infrastructure: that industrial systems operate under a constraint IT does not share, because a compromised network does not automatically have to become a catastrophic physical event. The argument is to move the security question upstream into design — identifying the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineering them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system remaining trustworthy. Aviation's safety culture already embeds the principle — independent systems, engineered fallbacks, defined degraded modes. The argument here is to apply it explicitly to airport and airline OT, asking where a network compromise could produce a physical or safety consequence and what design change would remove that possibility. This is practitioner analysis rather than incident reporting; it names no victim and describes no attack, but it is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure.

items.title: Google reports a financially motivated group running a full credential-harvesting campaign with autonomous agents in under six hours
items.content_text: Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported on 8 September that a financially motivated actor stood up and executed a large-scale credential-harvesting campaign in less than six hours using an autonomous multi-agent framework, with the agents handling stages that previously took an operator days. GTIG also observed actors going after proprietary AI models across healthcare, government and media, stealing API credentials and hijacking victim cloud tenants to run their own workloads on someone else’s bill. Its guidance is to assume every threat actor now uses AI somewhere in the chain. For airports and airlines the exposure is the credential estate around operations: crew and ground-handler portals, ground-support scheduling, maintenance and MRO tooling, and the federated identity that increasingly sits behind vendor access to terminal and airside systems.

items.title: Ukraine formally notifies aviation authorities that Russian airspace presents a growing risk to civil aircraft
items.content_text: Ukraine issued a formal notification to international aviation authorities on 2 September warning that Russian airspace carries growing risk to civil aviation, a day after President Zelenskyy urged airlines and insurers to stop using Russian airspace and airports as long-range drone operations expand. Russia’s civil aviation regulator rejected the warning. This is an airspace-safety and geopolitical matter rather than a cyber event, and most Western carriers have avoided the airspace since 2022 — but it belongs on an OT dashboard for one reason. The same operating environment has produced sustained regional GNSS jamming and spoofing, and navigation-integrity degradation is the point where an external, non-cyber disruption starts behaving like an attack on a safety system: correct equipment, wrong answers.

items.title: Eighteen frontier models were run at a real enterprise network — one completed the whole kill chain unaided
items.content_text: Booz Allen published its Cyber Weapon Index and an accompanying report on 4 September, grading eighteen frontier AI models on how much of an intrusion they can carry out without a human driving. The models were run against a representative enterprise network rather than a benchmark; the top performer completed the full sequence — reconnaissance, initial access, lateral movement and objective — unaided, while most managed individual stages. The authors’ conclusion is about time rather than novelty: nothing in the tested behaviour was a new technique, but the interval between a foothold and a consequence compresses when the attacker never pauses to think. Booz Allen also reports that defensive playbooks written specifically against autonomous attackers cut their success rate by more than 95% in the same tests. For an airport the implication is the overnight window — baggage, fuelling and BMS controls sit behind facility networks that are watched hardest during the operating day, not at 3 am.
tags: Research — measured autonomous attack capability in frontier AI models; no incident

items.title: Six steps to being able to disconnect airside systems — and a three-month planning horizon
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks published a practitioner summary on 2 September of the Five Eyes “CI Fortify” guidance released in late July, reducing it to six steps: identify vital systems and their dependencies; establish trust levels and connection maps; pre-build the separation points; create and test graduated isolation plans; retain visibility while isolated; and run post-isolation checks before reconnecting. For airports the first step is the awkward one, because so many vital systems belong to someone else — common-use check-in, baggage reconciliation, ground-handling platforms. The recent European airport disruptions showed manual fallback working for check-in but not scaling. Nozomi’s suggestion that operators plan to sustain isolated operations for up to three months is worth reading against airside plant specifically: BMS, access control and airfield lighting need to keep running whether or not the terminal IT estate does.

items.title: NCSC issues an alert: increased targeting of OT across multiple sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
items.content_text: The NCSC published a formal alert on 27 August stating it has seen increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK, by a range of threat actors, with some limited real-world disruption already resulting. It names no victims, actors or techniques, and it landed the same day Manchester Airports Group disclosed its breach — a coincidence of timing, not a link. Aviation is not called out, but the exposure the NCSC describes is the airport’s: a campus estate of controllers bought as part of a building fit-out, supported remotely by an OEM, and rarely re-surveyed. Baggage handling drives, jet bridge controllers, de-icing and fuelling telemetry, airfield lighting cabinets, stand equipment, BMS and access control all sit in that category, and the instruction not to assume they are unreachable from the internet without verifying it is the whole point of the alert.

items.title: Cisco’s network access control server has a CVSS 10 authentication bypass under active attack — this is the box that decides which devices get onto which airport network
items.content_text: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, a CVSS 10.0 flaw in Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC that lets an unauthenticated remote attacker bypass the web-based management interface through an API endpoint with insufficient authentication. Cisco states its PSIRT “is aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability.” All versions are affected; fixes are 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4. There are no workarounds — restricting management traffic with infrastructure access control lists is the only mitigation short of patching. CISA added the CVE to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 September with an unusually short three-day federal remediation deadline of 19 September, which has now passed. No attribution has been published and no critical-infrastructure or aviation targeting has been claimed. The reason it matters here is architectural rather than reported: where an airport or airline estate runs 802.1X and posture-based access control, ISE is the policy engine that decides which contractor laptop, handheld or engineering workstation lands on a terminal, baggage or airside VLAN — so administrative control of it is control of the segmentation itself.

items.title: Six flaws in Digital Watchdog VMAX video recorders, the top two at CVSS 9.6 — CISA lists Transportation Systems among the sectors that run them
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-258-01 on 15 September covering Digital Watchdog VMAX digital and network video recorders — the A1 G4, IP G4, A1 PLUS, VA1G4 and VG4 lines. Six CVEs are listed, led by CVE-2026-66890 and CVE-2026-66887 at CVSS 9.6, with CVE-2026-68070 and CVE-2026-68950 at 8.8 and two lower-rated issues at 6.8 and 6.5. CISA states that exploitation can give an attacker full administrative control of the recorder. Updated firmware is available from the vendor, and no exploitation has been reported. The sectors CISA names for this advisory are Commercial Facilities, Government Services and Facilities, Healthcare and Public Health, and Transportation Systems. That last one is why it is carried here: recorders of this class are ordinary physical-security infrastructure in terminals, car parks, cargo sheds and landside offices, they are frequently installed and maintained by a security integrator rather than by IT, and they sit on cabling that often runs into the same closets as access control. Nothing in the advisory names an airport — treat this as an inventory question, not an aviation incident.

items.title: CISA’s 17 September batch runs to seven advisories — none of them aviation; the highest scores are in Mitsubishi engineering software and Schneider Modicon M340 controllers
items.content_text: CISA released seven ICS advisories on Thursday 17 September, ICSA-26-260-01 through -07: Bransys ELD, Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings, Hitachi Energy FACTS Control Platform, Schneider Electric Modicon M340 controllers and communication modules, Schneider Electric NetBotz 5 (750 and 755), ABB Ability Edgenius, and Schneider Electric PowerChute Serial Shutdown. The highest score we can verify in the batch is CVE-2026-15688 in GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings, an authentication-algorithm weakness rated CVSS 8.8 under v3.1 and 8.7 under v4.0, affecting all versions of Mitsubishi’s PLC engineering software. The Bransys advisory covers three credential-handling issues in an electronic logging device — hardcoded MQTT credentials at 7.5, cleartext transmission at 5.9 and hardcoded FTP credentials at 5.3, fixed in Android 11.00.00 and iOS 1.1.54. CISA lists Transportation Systems on that advisory, but ELDs are commercial-trucking hours-of-service devices and we are not going to stretch them into an aviation finding. CISA’s machine-readable advisory files now carry detail for four more. ICSA-26-260-04 republishes Schneider’s August 2025 advisory for CVE-2025-6625, a crafted FTP command that can deny service on Modicon M340 controllers and X80 Ethernet modules (CVSS 7.5 v3.1, 8.7 v4; M340 firmware fixed in SV3.70). ICSA-26-260-05 covers NetBotz 5 command injection CVE-2026-13336 (6.4 v3.1, 7.3 v4) and SQL injection CVE-2026-13337, fixed in 5.6.0. ICSA-26-260-06 is the Linux kernel “Copy Fail” privilege escalation CVE-2026-31431 (7.8) in ABB Edgenius gateways, fixed in 3.2.4.1. ICSA-26-260-07 is CVE-2026-13348 in PowerChute Serial Shutdown, a missing limit on authentication attempts (5.3 v3.1, 6.9 v4); CISA’s remediation text says to upgrade to version 1.6, but the same advisory also lists 1.6 as affected, so confirm the fixed build against Schneider’s own advisory. The Hitachi Energy advisory (-03) was still not verifiable at generation time, and its scores are deliberately omitted rather than guessed. Separately, CISA updated ICSA-26-211-07 (Mitsubishi Electric CC-Link IE TSN) on the same day, adding eight affected products. No exploitation is reported for anything in the batch.

items.title: GitLab CVSS 10 path traversal is being exploited, and airport and airline teams host more of it than they think
items.content_text: GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706 on 10 September, a path-traversal flaw in the repository commits API that it rated CVSS 10.0 and that allows an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday 11 September with a remediation deadline for federal agencies of Monday 14 September. watchTowr reported it was already seeing in-the-wild probes for vulnerable servers, and Hong Kong’s CERT issued its own advisory on 14 September stating the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A second flaw fixed in the same release, CVE-2026-87719, can expose sensitive information from Enterprise Edition servers. Airport and airline estates version baggage-handling integrations, gate and stand allocation logic, BMS and access-control middleware, MRO systems and airline operations tooling in self-hosted GitLab. Unauthenticated file reads against those servers surface the service accounts and API keys that reach airside and terminal systems.

items.title: Nozomi finishes its Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 research: twelve flaws, several chainable to root on an OT edge device — patched, unexploited, and older than it looks
items.content_text: Correction to the previous edition. This entry previously read as a new critical disclosure dated 15 September. It was not. The underlying CVEs were disclosed in May 2025 under CISA advisory ICSA-25-135-18; what happened on 15 September was a CISA update to that advisory, adding the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client and vendor fixes. The research behind it published in two parts: the first, on 10 September, covered four PROFINET Discovery and basic Configuration Protocol memory-corruption flaws in the SCALANCE LPE9403 — an uninitialised value, a NULL pointer dereference and two out-of-bounds reads, each rated CVSS 5.3 and each a denial of service rather than code execution. The second part, published by Nozomi Networks Labs on 18 September, gives the full picture: twelve vulnerabilities in total, nine in the device firmware rated between 5.3 and 8.5 and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client rated between 6.7 and 8.5. Nozomi demonstrated that several of them can be chained to obtain root-level control of the device, which in an OT context means manipulating telemetry, suppressing alarms, reading operational data, disrupting services and moving laterally. Affected are LPE9403 firmware below V4.0 HF0 and the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client through V2.1; Siemens has published advisories and fixes, with V4.0 HF0 and later the fixed firmware. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. For aviation the relevance is where these devices sit: the LPE9403 is a local-processing engine used as a PROFINET edge collector, and where an integrator has put one into baggage, plant-room, BMS or airfield equipment, root on it is root inside the segment that equipment lives in.

_otthreatfeed.category: Research — Vendor-patched, no known exploitation

_otthreatfeed.date_note: CVEs disclosed May 2025; research published 10 and 18 Sep 2026; CISA advisory updated 15 Sep 2026

items.title: An APT cluster whose tooling overlaps Sandworm and a ransomware operator that deployed Qilin are exploiting Cisco firewall management — the boundary between airport IT and airfield OT
items.content_text: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is being exploited in the wild. The flaw is a critical authentication bypass caused by an improper system process created at boot; a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the underlying operating system. Cisco patched it in early March and added indicators of compromise in late July, then disclosed on 9 September that it had observed exploitation from August. CISA added the CVE to its KEV catalog with a 12 September federal deadline, which has now passed. Cisco Talos tracks three post-compromise clusters across this flaw and the earlier static-credential flaw CVE-2026-20316: UAT-12197, unattributed, which used CVE-2026-20079 to plant a web shell and a JAR-based command executor and exfiltrate credentials; UAT-11823, an APT that used both CVEs and is Sandworm-linked through tooling overlap, deploying a Cyclops Blink variant — Talos does not say Sandworm itself carried it out; and UAT-11988, which Talos assesses with high confidence to be a ransomware operator with TTPs consistent with Qilin affiliates, came in through CVE-2026-20316 alone, enumerated targets for encryption and deployed Qilin on selected endpoints. CVE-2026-20316 is not in the KEV catalogue. On 16 September Cisco shipped its September hardening release for ASA, FTD and FMC (CVE-2026-20329 to CVE-2026-20336, maximum CVSS 9.9), which accompanies the exploited FMC flaws. Airports should treat this as an airfield-and-terminal segmentation problem rather than an office IT patch. The firewalls FMC configures are usually what stands between the corporate network and baggage handling, jet bridges, fuelling, de-icing, airfield lighting, BMS and access control.

items.title: ScreenConnect is being used to push scripts to endpoints as they connect — the console your handlers and integrators already have on your estate
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-84869 in ConnectWise ScreenConnect to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 12 September with a federal remediation deadline of 14 September. The flaw is a missing authorisation check rated CVSS 9.9 that permits unauthorised file transfer and code execution, and three separate incidents have been documented in which threat actors abused it to push malicious scripts to endpoints as those endpoints newly connected to a server. That detail is the one that matters operationally: the malicious action arrives through the legitimate management channel, signed off by the tool the estate is built to trust, so it looks like maintenance rather than intrusion. ScreenConnect and its peers are the standing path by which ground handlers, baggage and BMS maintainers, access-control contractors and airport systems integrators reach terminal systems out of hours, frequently on instances the airport authority neither owns nor patches. It sits alongside this week’s other confirmed remote-access exploitation as a single theme: the attacker is no longer forcing a boundary, they are borrowing the support tool that already crosses it.

items.title: NetScaler is being probed harder than it is being patched — 56 exploitation attempts in a week against an authentication bypass now in KEV
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-19490 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 9 September, an authentication bypass rated CVSS 9.3 affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway in AAA virtual server and Gateway configurations, with a federal deadline of 12 September that has now passed. Honeypot telemetry logged 56 exploitation attempts from 3 September onward, 36 of them on 8 September alone, which is the shape of opportunistic mass scanning rather than targeted intrusion — internet-facing devices are being found and tried before their owners finish the change window. It arrived in the same KEV batch as the Fortinet FortiOS, FortiSwitchManager and FortiSASE heap overflow CVE-2025-25249, exploited since July and linked to a campaign that has infected an estimated 178 FortiGate devices with the PivotC2 remote access trojan. Aviation reads these as one exposure. NetScaler Gateway is a common front door for airline crew and operations portals, engineering and MRO applications and third-party access into terminal systems, and FortiGate is among the most common devices sitting on the boundary between an airport’s corporate network and its airside estate. An authentication bypass on either is not a data-theft problem, it is a segmentation problem.

items.title: MikroTik RouterOS “MikroTrick” chain moves from disclosed to confirmed exploited — CERT Polska
items.content_text: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS vulnerabilities known as the “MikroTrick” chain — previously disclosed but not confirmed exploited — are now being used in real-world attacks, with activity observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs an SSH authentication-bypass flaw, CVE-2026-67276 at CVSS 9.2, with an SSH privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-86060 also at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device; a third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure or denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. CERT Polska named no victims and no sectors, noting only that MikroTik hardware is widely deployed across ISPs, data centres, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks. That breadth is the aviation relevance rather than any confirmed airport targeting: RouterOS boxes turn up in the inexpensive, quietly-installed corners of an airport estate — remote stands and cargo sheds, car parks and shuttle depots, contractor site offices, CCTV and Wi-Fi backhaul — the places least likely to appear in an asset register and most likely to have an SSH port open for vendor support.

items.title: CISA adds four exploited flaws on 8 September, led by a CVSS 10 pre-auth RCE in the remote-monitoring platform many airport contractors run on
items.content_text: The 8 September KEV batch is headed by CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, a static code-injection flaw rated CVSS 10.0 that gives unauthenticated remote code execution. N-able has confirmed exploitation in the wild, Huntress observed attacks against the platform’s API and appliance logs from 4 September, and the vendor shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — its fourth hotfix in five weeks. Federal agencies have until 11 September. Also added: two Windows zero-days confirmed exploited on the same day, CVE-2026-81963 in the Update Stack and CVE-2026-85880 in ALPC, both giving SYSTEM, plus CVE-2026-75650 in Adobe Commerce. N-central matters here because it is a managed-service platform: at airports it is the sort of console an integrator uses to reach terminal building management, access control and baggage estates.
tags: Advisory — Four actively exploited flaws added to CISA KEV

items.title: September ICS Patch Tuesday: Siemens fixes an authentication bypass in protection relays, Schneider a critical flaw in Modicon M580
items.content_text: Siemens published nine advisories, seven of them on 8 September. The heaviest is SSA-142885 covering Reyrolle 7SR5 protection and control relays: fourteen CVEs in all versions before V2.70, led by CVE-2026-62645 at CVSS 9.8, where the web interface leaks enough information for an attacker to calculate current and past session identifiers and bypass authentication. Critical items also landed in Industrial Edge Management, Open Interface Services and SIMOVE Fleetmanager. Schneider Electric issued four advisories the same day, the most severe a critical authentication flaw in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety controllers, CVE-2026-3869 at CVSS 9.2, with high-severity fixes for PowerLogic T300 and EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert. Aveva patched four flaws in Pipeline Integrity Monitor, and CISA picked that one up separately on 10 September as ICSA-26-253-01: hard-coded cryptographic key CVE-2026-81821 and weak password hashing CVE-2026-81822, both CVSS 8.4, plus a missing-authorisation flaw at 5.3 and a cross-site scripting flaw at 4.7, in versions up to and including 2025 SP1 P1, fixed in the 2025 SP1 P2 security update. No exploitation has been reported for any of it.

items.title: CISA’s 3 September batch covers the contractor’s VPN client and the firmware tool — IXON, Rockwell ControlFLASH, Ignition
items.content_text: CISA published a further set of ICS advisories on 3 September. Three are relevant to airport facility and ground OT. ICSA-26-246-02 covers the IXON VPN Client, where CVE-2026-75925 allows remote code execution with elevated privileges on the machine running the client in versions before 1.4.7 — the standard arrangement for baggage-handling, jet-bridge and de-icing vendors who support kit remotely. ICSA-26-246-03 covers Rockwell Automation ControlFLASH at V15.07 and earlier, where CVE-2026-12663 lets commands or code run at the logged-in user’s permission level; ControlFLASH is the firmware tool for the controllers under baggage systems, fuelling and airfield plant. ICSA-26-246-06 covers Inductive Automation Ignition, where any authenticated user can create projects — Ignition appears as a visualisation layer over BMS and baggage telemetry. None is reported as exploited.

items.title: A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in SonicWall’s SMA1000 remote-access gateway is being exploited, and CISA gave agencies three days
items.content_text: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance are being exploited in the wild; the company says it found both the flaws and the exploitation internally. CVE-2026-83548, scored CVSS 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface. CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an operating-system command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console. Chained, the pair gives an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution on the appliance itself. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2 September with a 5 September deadline for federal civilian agencies, and marked both entries as requiring forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 — a signal that patching alone does not close the incident. Affected models are the SMA1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v; SSL-VPN running on SonicWall firewalls and the SMA 100 series are not affected.

items.title: CISA publishes a cyber-decoys guide — the rare detection control you can add to an airport network without touching what it controls
items.content_text: CISA released “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September. The guide defines decoys as assets that look like legitimate systems, accounts or data but exist to distract an adversary, reveal their presence, or collect intelligence on how they operate, and it sets out three phases: preparation, execution and analysis. CISA positions the technique alongside Zero Trust rather than as a replacement for it. The reason it reads well for aviation is the constraint every airport security team knows: you cannot install an agent on a baggage controller, a jet-bridge PLC or an airfield-lighting panel, and a change window on those systems is expensive. A decoy is additive — a fake engineering workstation, a planted credential that no legitimate process should ever use, a file share named to look like integrator documentation — and it produces a signal with almost no false positives, because nothing legitimate should touch it. The catch is that a decoy nobody monitors is decoration, so the alerting path matters more than the decoy.

items.title: CISA is retiring its weekly vulnerability bulletin on 28 September — a small change that breaks a lot of quiet Monday-morning routines
items.content_text: CISA will stop publishing its weekly Vulnerability Summary bulletin from 28 September, pointing readers instead to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, its alerts and its advisories. The agency frames the move as consistent with the risk-based prioritisation set out in binding operational directive BOD 26-04 of June 2026: a weekly digest of everything published is a poor instrument next to a catalog of what is actually being exploited. Nothing in the reporting indicates the ICS advisory stream is affected. It is worth flagging for aviation readers because the weekly bulletin is quietly load-bearing in small vulnerability-management routines — the airport or airline team without a dedicated threat-intel function that reads one email a week and triages from it. If that describes your process, the replacement is not a new email; it is a subscription to KEV and the ICS advisory feed, and a decision about who reads them and how often.

items.title: A US rule now counts a cyberattack as a “not controllable” cause of delay — and ties the relief to being compliant
items.content_text: A Department of Transportation rule reported on 11 September creates a new cause-of-delay category and designates ten types of disruption as “not controllable,” cyberattacks among them. Where a carrier is compliant with the cybersecurity regulations that apply to it, it no longer owes meals, hotels or comparable amenities under its customer service plan when one of those causes grounds flights; carriers that are not compliant remain subject to the requirements. Nothing here touches an aviation control system — this is advisory-only for OT. What it changes is the cost calculus behind a grounding cyber incident, and it puts a financial edge on being able to evidence compliance, because the carrier that can show it met its obligations is the one that keeps the relief. Reporting places the rule against the backdrop of the Scattered Spider intrusions at airlines, the Collins Aerospace incident that delayed European flights and the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, and notes there is no formal accounting of how often cyberattacks previously triggered compensation claims. Carried here factually as a regulatory change, with no comment on the policy debate around it.

items.title: ENISA switches on the Single Reporting Platform as the Cyber Resilience Act’s vulnerability reporting duties take effect
items.content_text: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity deployed the initial operating capability of its Single Reporting Platform, announced 14 September, giving manufacturers and open-source software stewards the channel they need to meet Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations that took effect this month. Under the CRA, makers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents on a defined clock, with an early warning followed by a fuller notification. Airports and airlines are mostly beneficiaries here, but suppliers of baggage, BMS, access-control and airfield equipment placing products on the EU market now carry an active-exploitation reporting duty with a hard clock on it. Reported here factually as a regulatory milestone, without comment on the underlying policy debate.

items.title: 117 federal cyber incident reporting rules across 27 agencies, and the argument that duplication costs you the first hours
items.content_text: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce, drawing on GAO figures, count 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations spread across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. Their argument is operational rather than administrative: in the first hours of an incident the same small group of people is asked to satisfy several overlapping reporting obligations on different clocks and in different formats, and that work is taken directly from response. The timing matters because CIRCIA rules are expected to be finalised this autumn. Aviation operators already sit under a dense stack — TSA security directives for regulated entities, CISA reporting, national aviation authority obligations, and separate data-protection notification duties as the Manchester case illustrated.

items.title: CISA and the G7 tell operators to start the post-quantum inventory now — the deadline is set by your asset lifetimes, not by them
items.content_text: CISA and the G7 Cyber Security Working Group issued a joint call on 4 September for governments and organisations to begin the transition to post-quantum cryptography, setting out a phased, risk-based approach: inventory the cryptography in use and the dependencies that carry it, identify the data and systems whose exposure would outlast the migration, and hold a written transition plan rather than a procurement wish. The statement is explicit about store-now-decrypt-later — traffic captured today can be decrypted later — and about the second-order problem, which is that authentication and firmware-signing chains rest on the same public-key algorithms. It is guidance, not a rule, and no deadline attaches. For an airport the relevance is lifecycle: BMS, access control and baggage systems specified this year will still be in service well past the migration window, and their firmware-signing and remote-access cryptography is fixed at purchase.
tags: Guidance — CISA and G7 joint call to begin the post-quantum cryptography transition; no deadline attached

items.title: Six agencies publish outage-communication guidance for IT and OT service providers — the gap the airport disruptions exposed
items.content_text: On 2 September the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security joined CISA, Australia’s ASD ACSC, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK and the FBI to publish joint guidance on communicating during IT and OT service outages, titled “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers.” It calls for a written incident communications plan with defined trigger thresholds and named audiences, plain-language updates, root-cause and technical detail end users can act on, and messaging aligned with legal and regulatory duties. Aviation has the clearest recent illustration of why this is an operational control rather than a communications nicety: shared check-in and baggage platforms mean a single supplier outage propagates across independent airports simultaneously, and the airports affected are left explaining a failure they did not cause and cannot directly diagnose.

items.title: Britain moves to bar designated high-risk suppliers from critical infrastructure — without naming them publicly
items.content_text: The UK government has tabled late amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill that would let ministers stop critical-sector organisations from using technology suppliers designated as high risk. The Bill, introduced in November 2025 and now near the end of its passage through the Lords, already extends duties to energy, water, transport and health operators and pulls managed service providers, data centres and digital infrastructure into scope. The amendments were tabled on 24 August and reported on 2 September; they follow reporting that a small UK generating station ran manually for four days after a cyberattack. Designations would not necessarily be made public, which is the detail operators should notice: a supplier could be designated without a public list to check against, so the obligation to know your own supply chain moves from good practice to compliance exposure. None of this is in force yet, and the Bill has not completed its passage.
